# json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/json/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#json-rust)json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](https://docs.rs/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

[§](https://docs.rs#why)Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = json::parse(r#"
{
    "code": 200,
    "success": true,
    "payload": {
        "features": [
            "awesome",
            "easyAPI",
            "lowLearningCurve"
        ]
    }
}
"#).unwrap();
let instantiated = object!{
    // quotes on keys are optional
    "code": 200,
    success: true,
    payload: {
        features: [
            "awesome",
            "easyAPI",
            "lowLearningCurve"
        ]
    }
};
assert_eq!(parsed, instantiated);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#first-class-citizen)First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it’s easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!{
    foo: false,
    bar: null,
    answer: 42,
    list: [null, "world", true]
};
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!(data["foo"] == false);
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!(data["bar"] != false);
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!(data["answer"] == 42);
assert!(data["answer"] == 42.0);
assert!(data["answer"] == 42isize);
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!(data["list"][0].is_null());
assert!(data["list"][1] == "world");
assert!(data["list"][2] == true);
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!(data["this"]["does"]["not"]["exist"].is_null());
// Mutate by assigning:
data["list"][0] = "Hello".into();
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"foo":false,"bar":null,"answer":42,"list":["Hello","world",true]}"#);
// Or pretty print it out:
println!("{:#}", data);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serialize-with-jsonstringifyvalue)Serialize with `json::stringify(value)`

Primitives:

```
// str slices
assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar"), "\"foobar\"");
// Owned strings
assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar".to_string()), "\"foobar\"");
// Any number types
assert_eq!(json::stringify(42), "42");
// Booleans
assert_eq!(json::stringify(true), "true");
assert_eq!(json::stringify(false), "false");
```
Explicit `null` type `json::Null`:

`assert_eq!(json::stringify(json::Null), "null");`Optional types:

```
let value: Option<String> = Some("foo".to_string());
assert_eq!(json::stringify(value), "\"foo\"");
let no_value: Option<String> = None;
assert_eq!(json::stringify(no_value), "null");
```
Vector:

```
let data = vec![1,2,3];
assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,2,3]");
```
Vector with optional values:

```
let data = vec![Some(1), None, Some(2), None, Some(3)];
assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,null,2,null,3]");
```
Pushing to arrays:

```
let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_array();
data.push(10);
data.push("foo");
data.push(false);
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"[10,"foo",false]"#);
```
Putting fields on objects:

```
let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_object();
data["answer"] = 42.into();
data["foo"] = "bar".into();
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"answer":42,"foo":"bar"}"#);
```
`array!` macro:

```
let data = array!["foo", "bar", 100, true, null];
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"["foo","bar",100,true,null]"#);
```
`object!` macro:

```
let data = object!{
    name: "John Doe",
    age: 30,
    canJSON: true
};
assert_eq!(
    data.dump(),
    r#"{"name":"John Doe","age":30,"canJSON":true}"#
);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [array](https://docs.rs/macro.array.html)
- Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Array`.
- [object](https://docs.rs/macro.object.html)
- Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Object`.
- [value](https://docs.rs/macro.value.html)
- Helper crate for converting types into `JsonValue`. It’s used internally by the`object!`and`array!`macros.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from](https://docs.rs/fn.from.html)
- Convenience for `JsonValue::from(value)`
- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- [stringify](https://docs.rs/fn.stringify.html)
- Pretty prints out the value as JSON string.
- [stringify_](https://docs.rs/fn.stringify_pretty.html)- pretty
- Pretty prints out the value as JSON string. Second argument is a number of spaces to indent new blocks with.

---

# json 0.12.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/latest

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](https://docs.rs/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```
## Performance and Conformance

There used to be a statement here saying that performance is not the main goal of this crate. It is definitely one of them now.

While this crate doesn't provide a way to parse JSON to native Rust structs, it does a
lot to optimize its performance for DOM parsing, stringifying and manipulation. It does
[very well in benchmarks](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark), in some cases it
can even outperform parsing to structs.

This crate implements the standard according to the [
RFC 7159](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7159) and
[ECMA-404](http://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf)
documents. For the best interoperability numbers are treated stored as 64bit precision
mantissa with 16 bit decimal exponent for floating point representation.

## License

This crate is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0). Choose whichever one works best for you.

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# smooth_operator_adapter_postgres - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-postgres/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_postgres/

## Expand description

Postgres + pgvector [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the dogfood backend.

This is the production Postgres implementation of the one storage seam (see
`docs/STORAGE.md`). It mirrors the smooai monorepo’s schema so dogfooding is
a swap, not a rewrite:

- **OLTP**(conversations / participants / messages / sessions): async CRUD over a- `deadpool_postgres`
- **Checkpoints**: smooth-operator’s- `PostgresCheckpointStore`- *synchronous*r2d2-pooled store) constructed against the- **same database**— so the engine’s- `with_checkpoint_store`plugs straight in and agent state lives next to the conversations it belongs to.
- **Knowledge**: a pgvector-backed- `PgKnowledgeBase`- `tsvector`BM25 → Reciprocal Rank Fusion). Text→vector goes through the- `Embedder`- `DeterministicEmbedder`- `GatewayEmbedder`
- **Memory**: a pgvector-backed- `PgMemory`- `(organization_id, user_id)`like the TS- `['memories', orgId, userId]`store. Implements the core- `Memory`- `Embedder`

[§](https://docs.rs#sharing-one-database-between-the-async-pool-and-the-sync-checkpoint-store)Sharing one database between the async pool and the sync checkpoint store

The OLTP/knowledge slices need async (`tokio-postgres` + `deadpool`); the
checkpoint slice is a sync trait backed by an r2d2 pool inside
smooth-operator. Both are pointed at the **same  conn_str**: we build the
async deadpool from it for our own queries, and hand the

*same*string to

`PostgresCheckpointStore::connect`, which stands up its own small r2d2 pool
and `checkpoints` table in that database. Two pools, two driver stacks, one
Postgres — the tables coexist (ours from [`schema`], theirs from their own
`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`).## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deterministic](https://docs.rs/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)- Embedder
- Deterministic, network-free pseudo-embedder.
- [Gateway](https://docs.rs/struct.GatewayEmbedder.html)- Embedder
- OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings`embedder (the SmooAI LiteLLM gateway).
- [Gateway](https://docs.rs/struct.GatewayReranker.html)- Reranker
- Cross-encoder reranker over the SmooAI gateway’s `/v1/rerank`endpoint (feature gap G8).
- [Http](https://docs.rs/struct.HttpRerankBackend.html)- Rerank - Backend
- The real backend: a Cohere/Voyage-style `/v1/rerank`call over the gateway.
- [PgAgent](https://docs.rs/struct.PgAgentConfigResolver.html)- Config - Resolver
- Postgres-backed `AgentConfigResolver``agents`table.
- [PgConnector](https://docs.rs/struct.PgConnectorConfigStore.html)- Config - Store
- Postgres-backed `ConnectorConfigStore``connector_configs`.
- [PgIndexing](https://docs.rs/struct.PgIndexingStore.html)- Store
- Postgres-backed `IndexingStore``indexing_runs`.
- [PgKnowledge](https://docs.rs/struct.PgKnowledgeBase.html)- Base
- pgvector knowledge base. Cheap to clone (all fields are `Arc`/pool handles).
- [PgMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.PgMemory.html)
- pgvector-backed agent memory, bound to one `(organization_id, user_id)`namespace. Cheap to clone (all fields are`Arc`/pool handles + small strings).
- [PgSettings](https://docs.rs/struct.PgSettingsStore.html)- Store
- Postgres-backed `SettingsStore``agent_settings`.
- [Postgres](https://docs.rs/struct.PostgresAdapter.html)- Adapter
- Postgres + pgvector storage adapter.
- [Rerank](https://docs.rs/struct.RerankScore.html)- Score
- One scored candidate returned by a `RerankBackend``documents`array, and its relevance score against the query.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Input](https://docs.rs/enum.InputType.html)- Type
- Whether an embedding is for a document being stored or a search query.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_EMBEDDING_DIM.html)- EMBEDDING_ - DIM
- Default embedding dimension (Voyage `voyage-3-large`shape; mirrors smooai’s`knowledge_vectors embedding vector(1024)`).
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_RERANK_MODEL.html)- RERANK_ - MODEL
- Default rerank model requested over the gateway (Cohere-compatible). Distinct from the embedding model and the chat model.
- [OPENAI_](https://docs.rs/constant.OPENAI_SMALL_EMBEDDING_DIM.html)- SMALL_ - EMBEDDING_ - DIM
- Dimension returned by OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Embedder](https://docs.rs/trait.Embedder.html)
- Turn text into dense vectors. Implementations must return one vector per
input string, each of length `Embedder::dim`
- [Rerank](https://docs.rs/trait.RerankBackend.html)- Backend
- A pluggable rerank backend.

# smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_nats - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-backplane-nats/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_nats/

## Expand description

NATS [ Backplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/trait.Backplane.html) — cross-pod scale-out + a shared event bus.

Same shape as the Redis adapter (a per-pod [ InMemoryBackplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html) for local
registry + delivery, plus a bus for cross-pod fan-out) but over NATS subjects.
NATS is attractive here beyond raw fan-out: queue groups, JetStream
persistence/replay, and the fact that the same broker doubles as the
platform’s multi-channel event bus — so non-AI publishers (job status,
ingestion progress, notifications) and other services can share it.

Per call:

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Nats](https://docs.rs/struct.NatsBackplane.html)- Backplane
- A `Backplane``publish`out across pods over NATS.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_SUBJECT.html)- SUBJECT
- Default subject. Override via `NatsBackplane::connect_on_subject`

---

# smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_redis - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-backplane-redis/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_redis/

## Expand description

Redis / Valkey [ Backplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/trait.Backplane.html) — the horizontal scale-out seam.

The default [ InMemoryBackplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html) only reaches sockets held by the current
process, so with more than one replica an event produced on pod A can’t reach
a socket on pod B.

[closes that gap](https://docs.rs/struct.RedisBackplane.html)

`RedisBackplane`**without changing the trait or any call site**: it keeps a per-pod

[for the local registry + delivery, and adds a Redis pub/sub bus for cross-pod fan-out.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html)

`InMemoryBackplane`Per call:

- `attach`- `detach`- `associate`- **local**— a connection lives on exactly one pod, so only that pod registers it.
- `publish`- `BackplaneEnvelope`- `Target`- *its own*registry and delivers to its sockets — so the same- `publish`call fans out across the whole fleet. The origin pod skips its own echo (it already delivered).

This is the classic pub/sub fan-out (the shape Socket.IO’s Redis adapter uses): no shared connection registry, each pod authoritative for its own sockets.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Redis](https://docs.rs/struct.RedisBackplane.html)- Backplane
- A `Backplane``publish`out across pods over Redis/Valkey pub/sub.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_CHANNEL.html)- CHANNEL
- Default pub/sub channel. Override via `RedisBackplane::connect_on_channel`

# smooth_operator_adapter_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-memory/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_memory/

## Expand description

In-memory [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the conformance / test baseline.

All OLTP slices (conversations, participants, messages, sessions) live in
`HashMap`s behind a single `RwLock`. The checkpoint and knowledge slices
delegate to smooth-operator’s own [ MemoryCheckpointStore](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/checkpoint/struct.MemoryCheckpointStore.html) and

[, which are exactly what the engine expects — so this adapter is a faithful (if non-durable) stand-in for Postgres/DynamoDB.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/knowledge/struct.InMemoryKnowledge.html)

`InMemoryKnowledge`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [InMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.InMemoryStorageAdapter.html)- Storage - Adapter
- In-memory storage adapter. Cheap to clone is *not*a goal — wrap in`Arc`for sharing.

# smooth_operator_ingestion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-ingestion/1.11.1/smooth_operator_ingestion/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator-ingestion)smooth-operator ingestion

Knowledge **ingestion + connectors** for smooth-operator — the pipeline
that pulls documents from a source, chunks them, embeds them, and stores them
in the [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html)
knowledge slice so they are retrievable. This closes feature gap G1 (knowledge
ingestion + connectors), G2 (document chunking pipeline), and G9 (the
connector mock +

`unit`-vs-`external` test split). See `docs/INGESTION.md`.[§](https://docs.rs#shape)Shape

```
Connector::pull ─▶ Chunker::chunk ─▶ Embedder::embed ─▶ KnowledgeBase::ingest
   RawDocument        Vec<Chunk>        Vec<Vec<f32>>        (StorageAdapter
                                                              knowledge slice)
```
- `Connector`- `RawDocument`- `pull(since)`). Built-ins:- `FileConnector`- `WebConnector`- `MockConnector`
- `Chunker`
- `Embedder`- `smooth_operator::embedding`- `DeterministicEmbedder`
- `ingest`- `(doc id, content hash)`via an- `IngestLedger`

[§](https://docs.rs#wiring-example)Wiring example

```
let connector = FileConnector::new("./docs");
let report = ingest(
    &connector,
    &Chunker::default(),
    &DeterministicEmbedder::new(),
    storage.knowledge(),
    IngestOptions::for_org("org-acme"),
)
.await?;
println!("stored {} chunks", report.chunks_stored);
```

# smooth_operator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/smooth_operator/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator)smooth-operator

The reference core for smooth-operator — the service layer on top of
[ smooth_operator_core](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/index.html) (the agent engine). It defines three things:

- `domain`- `spec/domain/*.json`. Checkpoints re-use the engine’s- `smooth_operator_core::Checkpoint`
- `adapter`- `StorageAdapter`- `docs/STORAGE.md`). Its checkpoint/knowledge accessors return smooth-operator-core’s own traits so the engine plugs straight in.
- `runtime`- `AgentRuntime`- `Agent`- `Workflow`

It also owns two shared retrieval seams both backends/consumers depend on:
[ embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html) (the text→vector

[+ the network-free](https://docs.rs/embedding/trait.Embedder.html)

`Embedder`[, the one home for both the Postgres adapter and the ingestion pipeline) and](https://docs.rs/embedding/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)

`DeterministicEmbedder`[(the optional post-retrieval](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)

`rerank`[stage — feature gap G8).](https://docs.rs/rerank/trait.Reranker.html)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [access_](https://docs.rs/access_control/index.html)- control
- Document-level access control (feature gap G3).
- [adapter](https://docs.rs/adapter/index.html)
- The `StorageAdapter`seam.
- [agent_](https://docs.rs/agent_config/index.html)- config
- Per-agent behavior config (SMOODEV-590 parity in Rust).
- [auth](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)
- Authentication + role-based access control (Phase 12).
- [backplane](https://docs.rs/backplane/index.html)
- Connection backplane: the scale-out + event-delivery seam for the WebSocket server.
- [connector_](https://docs.rs/connector_config/index.html)- config
- Connector configuration storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [curation](https://docs.rs/curation/index.html)
- Document sets, curation boosting, and query-time metadata filters (feature gap, Phase 11 — “Document sets / curation / boosting”).
- [domain](https://docs.rs/domain/index.html)
- Domain model for smooth-operator.
- [embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html)
- Text → vector embedding — the shared seam for dense retrieval.
- [gateway_](https://docs.rs/gateway_key/index.html)- key
- Per-org LLM gateway-key resolution: the seam that lets a multi-tenant
deployment bill/scope each org’s turns to its **own**gateway key while a standalone/local server keeps using the single environment key.
- [otp](https://docs.rs/otp/index.html)
- End-user identity verification (OTP) — the seam that lets a host wire a
one-time-code flow behind a public agent’s `end_user`tool auth, while the reference server stays credential-free.
- [rerank](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)
- Reranking — the optional post-retrieval reorder stage (feature gap G8).
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Minimal `AgentRuntime`that proves smooth-operator consumes smooth-operator.
- [settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html)
- Per-org agent settings storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [telemetry](https://docs.rs/telemetry/index.html)
- OpenTelemetry GenAI instrumentation for the agent turn.
- [tool_](https://docs.rs/tool_provider/index.html)- provider
- Host-contributed tool injection seam.
- [tools](https://docs.rs/tools/index.html)
- Tools the smooth-operator runtime registers on the smooth-operator-core engine.
- [widget_](https://docs.rs/widget_auth/index.html)- auth
- Embeddable-widget auth: an origin allowlist + public-key `authContext`verification for browser-embedded chat widgets (`<smooth-agent-chat>`).

# stop - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stop-cli/0.0.2/stop/

## Expand description

Process and system monitoring with structured output.

Provides cross-platform system metrics collection with filtering, sorting, and multiple output formats (JSON, CSV, human-readable).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use data::`- [DEFAULT_TOP_N](https://docs.rs/data/constant.DEFAULT_TOP_N.html);
- `pub use data::`- [ProcessInfo](https://docs.rs/data/struct.ProcessInfo.html);
- `pub use data::`- [SystemMetrics](https://docs.rs/data/struct.SystemMetrics.html);
- `pub use data::`- [SystemSnapshot](https://docs.rs/data/struct.SystemSnapshot.html);
- `pub use data::`- [collect_snapshot](https://docs.rs/data/fn.collect_snapshot.html);
- `pub use error::`- [StopError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.StopError.html);
- `pub use filter::`- [FilterExpr](https://docs.rs/filter/enum.FilterExpr.html);
- `pub use output::`- [Output](https://docs.rs/output/enum.Output.html);
- `pub use output::`- [ignore_broken_pipe](https://docs.rs/output/fn.ignore_broken_pipe.html);
- `pub use pipeline::`- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/pipeline/struct.Pipeline.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Data types and collection for system snapshots.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types for the stop CLI tool.
- [filter](https://docs.rs/filter/index.html)
- Filter expression parsing and evaluation for process queries.
- [output](https://docs.rs/output/index.html)
- Output formatting: structured (JSON, CSV) and human-readable display.
- [pipeline](https://docs.rs/pipeline/index.html)
- Process filtering pipeline: search → filter → sort → truncate.
- [watch](https://docs.rs/watch/index.html)
- Continuous monitoring (watch mode).

- [SetPsm](https://docs.rs/struct.SetPsmStorageVersionV2.html)- Storage - Version - V2
- One-shot migration: writes `pallet_psm`’s on-chain storage version to v2. Required because`RemovePallet<PsmName>`(above in the migration tuple) wipes the pallet’s`:__STORAGE_VERSION__:`key, and`InitializePsm`doesn’t re-seed it. Without this, try-runtime’s post-upgrade check sees in-code = 2, on-chain = 0 and panics.

# json 0.12.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.12.4

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](https://docs.rs/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```
## Performance and Conformance

There used to be a statement here saying that performance is not the main goal of this crate. It is definitely one of them now.

While this crate doesn't provide a way to parse JSON to native Rust structs, it does a
lot to optimize its performance for DOM parsing, stringifying and manipulation. It does
[very well in benchmarks](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark), in some cases it
can even outperform parsing to structs.

This crate implements the standard according to the [
RFC 7159](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7159) and
[ECMA-404](http://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf)
documents. For the best interoperability numbers are treated stored as 64bit precision
mantissa with 16 bit decimal exponent for floating point representation.

## License

This crate is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0). Choose whichever one works best for you.

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

---

                    json 0.12.4

                JSON implementation in Rust

# json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.12.4/target-redirect/json/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#json-rust)json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](https://docs.rs/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

[§](https://docs.rs#why)Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = json::parse(r#"
{
    "code": 200,
    "success": true,
    "payload": {
        "features": [
            "awesome",
            "easyAPI",
            "lowLearningCurve"
        ]
    }
}
"#).unwrap();
let instantiated = object!{
    // quotes on keys are optional
    "code": 200,
    success: true,
    payload: {
        features: [
            "awesome",
            "easyAPI",
            "lowLearningCurve"
        ]
    }
};
assert_eq!(parsed, instantiated);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#first-class-citizen)First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it’s easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!{
    foo: false,
    bar: null,
    answer: 42,
    list: [null, "world", true]
};
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!(data["foo"] == false);
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!(data["bar"] != false);
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!(data["answer"] == 42);
assert!(data["answer"] == 42.0);
assert!(data["answer"] == 42isize);
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!(data["list"][0].is_null());
assert!(data["list"][1] == "world");
assert!(data["list"][2] == true);
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!(data["this"]["does"]["not"]["exist"].is_null());
// Mutate by assigning:
data["list"][0] = "Hello".into();
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"foo":false,"bar":null,"answer":42,"list":["Hello","world",true]}"#);
// Or pretty print it out:
println!("{:#}", data);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serialize-with-jsonstringifyvalue)Serialize with `json::stringify(value)`

Primitives:

```
// str slices
assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar"), "\"foobar\"");
// Owned strings
assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar".to_string()), "\"foobar\"");
// Any number types
assert_eq!(json::stringify(42), "42");
// Booleans
assert_eq!(json::stringify(true), "true");
assert_eq!(json::stringify(false), "false");
```
Explicit `null` type `json::Null`:

`assert_eq!(json::stringify(json::Null), "null");`Optional types:

```
let value: Option<String> = Some("foo".to_string());
assert_eq!(json::stringify(value), "\"foo\"");
let no_value: Option<String> = None;
assert_eq!(json::stringify(no_value), "null");
```
Vector:

```
let data = vec![1,2,3];
assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,2,3]");
```
Vector with optional values:

```
let data = vec![Some(1), None, Some(2), None, Some(3)];
assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,null,2,null,3]");
```
Pushing to arrays:

```
let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_array();
data.push(10);
data.push("foo");
data.push(false);
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"[10,"foo",false]"#);
```
Putting fields on objects:

```
let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_object();
data["answer"] = 42.into();
data["foo"] = "bar".into();
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"answer":42,"foo":"bar"}"#);
```
`array!` macro:

```
let data = array!["foo", "bar", 100, true, null];
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"["foo","bar",100,true,null]"#);
```
`object!` macro:

```
let data = object!{
    name: "John Doe",
    age: 30,
    canJSON: true
};
assert_eq!(
    data.dump(),
    r#"{"name":"John Doe","age":30,"canJSON":true}"#
);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [array](https://docs.rs/macro.array.html)
- Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Array`.
- [object](https://docs.rs/macro.object.html)
- Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Object`.
- [value](https://docs.rs/macro.value.html)
- Helper crate for converting types into `JsonValue`. It’s used internally by the`object!`and`array!`macros.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from](https://docs.rs/fn.from.html)
- Convenience for `JsonValue::from(value)`
- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- [stringify](https://docs.rs/fn.stringify.html)
- Pretty prints out the value as JSON string.
- [stringify_](https://docs.rs/fn.stringify_pretty.html)- pretty
- Pretty prints out the value as JSON string. Second argument is a number of spaces to indent new blocks with.

[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! ```
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! // str slices
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar"), "\"foobar\"");
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! // Owned strings
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar".to_string()), "\"foobar\"");
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! // Any number types
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(42), "42");
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! // Booleans
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(true), "true");
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(false), "false");
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! ```
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! Explicit `null` type `json::Null`:
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! ```
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(json::Null), "null");
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! ```
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! Optional types:
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! let value: Option<String> = Some("foo".to_string());
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(value), "\"foo\"");
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! let no_value: Option<String> = None;
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(no_value), "null");
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! ```
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! Vector:
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! ```
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! let data = vec![1,2,3];
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,2,3]");
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! ```
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! Vector with optional values:
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! ```
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! let data = vec![Some(1), None, Some(2), None, Some(3)];
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,null,2,null,3]");
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! ```
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! Pushing to arrays:
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! ```
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_array();
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! data.push(10);
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! data.push("foo");
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! data.push(false);
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"[10,"foo",false]"#);
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! ```
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! Putting fields on objects:
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! ```
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_object();
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! data["answer"] = 42.into();
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! data["foo"] = "bar".into();
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"answer":42,"foo":"bar"}"#);
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! ```
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! `array!` macro:
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! ```
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! # #[macro_use] extern crate json;
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! # fn main() {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! let data = array!["foo", "bar", 100, true, null];
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"["foo","bar",100,true,null]"#);
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! # }
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! ```
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! `object!` macro:
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! ```
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! # #[macro_use] extern crate json;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! # fn main() {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! let data = object!{
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!     name: "John Doe",
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!     age: 30,
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!     canJSON: true
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! };
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! assert_eq!(
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!     data.dump(),
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!     r#"{"name":"John Doe","age":30,"canJSON":true}"#
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! );
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! # }
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! ```

}Create an empty `JsonValue::Object` instance.
When creating an object with data, consider using the `object!` macro.

Create an empty `JsonValue::Array` instance.
When creating array with data, consider using the `array!` macro.

Prints out the value as JSON string.

Pretty prints out the value as JSON string. Takes an argument that’s
number of spaces to indent new blocks with.

👎 Deprecated since 0.10.2: use `JsonValue::write` instead

 Writes the JSON as byte stream into an implementor of `std::io::Write`.

This method is deprecated as it will panic on io errors, use `write` instead.

Writes the JSON as byte stream into an implementor of `std::io::Write`.

Checks whether the value is empty. Returns true for:

empty string (`""`)
number `0`
boolean `false`
null
empty array (`array![]`)
empty object (`object!{}`)

Obtain an integer at a fixed decimal point. This is useful for
converting monetary values and doing arithmetic on them without
rounding errors introduced by floating point operations.

Will return `None` if `Number` called on a value that’s not a number,
or if the number is negative or a NaN.

let  price_a = JsonValue::from(5.99 );
let  price_b = JsonValue::from(7 );
let  price_c = JsonValue::from(10.2 );
assert_eq! (price_a.as_fixed_point_u64(2 ), Some (599 ));
assert_eq! (price_b.as_fixed_point_u64(2 ), Some (700 ));
assert_eq! (price_c.as_fixed_point_u64(2 ), Some (1020 ));Analog to `as_fixed_point_u64`, except returning a signed
`i64`, properly handling negative numbers.

let  balance_a = JsonValue::from(-1.49 );
let  balance_b = JsonValue::from(42 );
assert_eq! (balance_a.as_fixed_point_i64(2 ), Some (-149 ));
assert_eq! (balance_b.as_fixed_point_i64(2 ), Some (4200 ));Take over the ownership of the value, leaving `Null` in it’s place.

§ Examplelet  mut  data = array! ["Foo" , 42 ];
let  first = data[0 ].take();
let  second = data[1 ].take();
assert! (first == "Foo" );
assert! (second == 42 );
assert! (data[0 ].is_null());
assert! (data[1 ].is_null());Checks that self is a string, returns an owned Rust `String`, leaving
`Null` in it’s place.

If the contained string is already a heap allocated `String`, then
the ownership is moved without any heap allocation.

If the contained string is a `Short`, this will perform a heap
allocation to convert the types for you.

§ Examplelet  mut  data = array! ["Hello" , "World" ];
let  owned = data[0 ].take_string().expect("Should be a string" );
assert_eq! (owned, "Hello" );
assert! (data[0 ].is_null());Works on `JsonValue::Array` - pushes a new value to the array.

Works on `JsonValue::Array` - remove and return last element from
an array. On failure returns a null.

Works on `JsonValue::Array` - checks if the array contains a value

Works on `JsonValue::Object` - checks if the object has a key

Returns length of array or object (number of keys), defaults to `0` for
other types.

Works on `JsonValue::Array` - returns an iterator over members.
Will return an empty iterator if called on non-array types.

Works on `JsonValue::Array` - returns a mutable iterator over members.
Will return an empty iterator if called on non-array types.

Works on `JsonValue::Object` - returns an iterator over key value pairs.
Will return an empty iterator if called on non-object types.

Works on `JsonValue::Object` - returns a mutable iterator over
key value pairs.
Will return an empty iterator if called on non-object types.

Works on `JsonValue::Object` - inserts a new entry, or override an existing
one into the object. Note that `key` has to be a `&str` slice and not an owned
`String`. The internals of `Object` will handle the heap allocation of the key
if needed for better performance.

Works on `JsonValue::Object` - remove a key and return the value it held.
If the key was not present, the method is called on anything but an
object, it will return a null.

Works on `JsonValue::Array` - remove an entry and return the value it held.
If the method is called on anything but an object or if the index is out of bounds, it
will return `JsonValue::Null`.

When called on an array or an object, will wipe them clean. When called
on a string will clear the string. Numbers and booleans become null.

Performs copy-assignment from

`source`.

# array in json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/json/0.12.4/json/macro.array.html

```
macro_rules! array {
    [] => { ... };
    [@ITEM($( $i:expr, )*) $item:tt, $( $cont:tt )+] => { ... };
    (@ITEM($( $i:expr, )*) $item:tt,) => { ... };
    (@ITEM($( $i:expr, )*) $item:tt) => { ... };
    [@ITEM($( $i:expr, )*) $item:expr, $( $cont:tt )+] => { ... };
    (@ITEM($( $i:expr, )*) $item:expr,) => { ... };
    (@ITEM($( $i:expr, )*) $item:expr) => { ... };
    (@END $( $i:expr, )*) => { ... };
    ($( $cont:tt )+) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Array`.

```
let data = array!["foo", 42, false];
assert_eq!(data[0], "foo");
assert_eq!(data[1], 42);
assert_eq!(data[2], false);
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"["foo",42,false]"#);
```

---

# object in json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/json/0.12.4/json/macro.object.html

```
macro_rules! object {
    {} => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:ident: $( $cont:tt )*) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:literal: $( $cont:tt )*) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) [$key:expr]: $( $cont:tt )*) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:expr => $value:tt, $( $cont:tt )+) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:expr => $value:tt,) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:expr => $value:tt) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:expr => $value:expr, $( $cont:tt )+) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:expr => $value:expr,) => { ... };
    (@ENTRY($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) $key:expr => $value:expr) => { ... };
    (@END $( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) => { ... };
    ($key:tt: $( $cont:tt )+) => { ... };
    ($( $k:expr => $v:expr, )*) => { ... };
    ($( $k:expr => $v:expr ),*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Object`.

```
let data = object!{
    foo: 42,
    bar: false,
};
assert_eq!(data["foo"], 42);
assert_eq!(data["bar"], false);
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"foo":42,"bar":false}"#);
```

# value in json - Rust

macro_rules! value {
    ( null ) => { ... };

    ( {$( $token:tt )*} ) => { ... };
    { $value:expr } => { ... };

# json - Rust

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#json-rust)json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](https://docs.rs/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

[§](https://docs.rs#why)Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = json::parse(r#"
{
    "code": 200,
    "success": true,
    "payload": {
        "features": [
            "awesome",
            "easyAPI",
            "lowLearningCurve"
        ]
    }
}
"#).unwrap();
let instantiated = object!{
    // quotes on keys are optional
    "code": 200,
    success: true,
    payload: {
        features: [
            "awesome",
            "easyAPI",
            "lowLearningCurve"
        ]
    }
};
assert_eq!(parsed, instantiated);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#first-class-citizen)First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it’s easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!{
    foo: false,
    bar: null,
    answer: 42,
    list: [null, "world", true]
};
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!(data["foo"] == false);
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!(data["bar"] != false);
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!(data["answer"] == 42);
assert!(data["answer"] == 42.0);
assert!(data["answer"] == 42isize);
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!(data["list"][0].is_null());
assert!(data["list"][1] == "world");
assert!(data["list"][2] == true);
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!(data["this"]["does"]["not"]["exist"].is_null());
// Mutate by assigning:
data["list"][0] = "Hello".into();
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"foo":false,"bar":null,"answer":42,"list":["Hello","world",true]}"#);
// Or pretty print it out:
println!("{:#}", data);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serialize-with-jsonstringifyvalue)Serialize with `json::stringify(value)`

Primitives:

```
// str slices
assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar"), "\"foobar\"");
// Owned strings
assert_eq!(json::stringify("foobar".to_string()), "\"foobar\"");
// Any number types
assert_eq!(json::stringify(42), "42");
// Booleans
assert_eq!(json::stringify(true), "true");
assert_eq!(json::stringify(false), "false");
```
Explicit `null` type `json::Null`:

`assert_eq!(json::stringify(json::Null), "null");`Optional types:

```
let value: Option<String> = Some("foo".to_string());
assert_eq!(json::stringify(value), "\"foo\"");
let no_value: Option<String> = None;
assert_eq!(json::stringify(no_value), "null");
```
Vector:

```
let data = vec![1,2,3];
assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,2,3]");
```
Vector with optional values:

```
let data = vec![Some(1), None, Some(2), None, Some(3)];
assert_eq!(json::stringify(data), "[1,null,2,null,3]");
```
Pushing to arrays:

```
let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_array();
data.push(10);
data.push("foo");
data.push(false);
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"[10,"foo",false]"#);
```
Putting fields on objects:

```
let mut data = json::JsonValue::new_object();
data["answer"] = 42.into();
data["foo"] = "bar".into();
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"{"answer":42,"foo":"bar"}"#);
```
`array!` macro:

```
let data = array!["foo", "bar", 100, true, null];
assert_eq!(data.dump(), r#"["foo","bar",100,true,null]"#);
```
`object!` macro:

```
let data = object!{
    name: "John Doe",
    age: 30,
    canJSON: true
};
assert_eq!(
    data.dump(),
    r#"{"name":"John Doe","age":30,"canJSON":true}"#
);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [array](https://docs.rs/macro.array.html)
- Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Array`.
- [object](https://docs.rs/macro.object.html)
- Helper macro for creating instances of `JsonValue::Object`.
- [value](https://docs.rs/macro.value.html)
- Helper crate for converting types into `JsonValue`. It’s used internally by the`object!`and`array!`macros.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from](https://docs.rs/fn.from.html)
- Convenience for `JsonValue::from(value)`
- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- [stringify](https://docs.rs/fn.stringify.html)
- Pretty prints out the value as JSON string.
- [stringify_](https://docs.rs/fn.stringify_pretty.html)- pretty
- Pretty prints out the value as JSON string. Second argument is a number of spaces to indent new blocks with.

---

# json 0.12.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

---

# json 0.12.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.12.3

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](https://docs.rs/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```
## Performance and Conformance

There used to be a statement here saying that performance is not the main goal of this crate. It is definitely one of them now.

While this crate doesn't provide a way to parse JSON to native Rust structs, it does a
lot to optimize its performance for DOM parsing, stringifying and manipulation. It does
[very well in benchmarks](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark), in some cases it
can even outperform parsing to structs.

This crate implements the standard according to the [
RFC 7159](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7159) and
[ECMA-404](http://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf)
documents. For the best interoperability numbers are treated stored as 64bit precision
mantissa with 16 bit decimal exponent for floating point representation.

## License

This crate is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0). Choose whichever one works best for you.

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

---

documents. For the best interoperability numbers are treated stored as 64bit precision
mantissa with 16 bit decimal exponent for floating point representation.

# json 0.11.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.11.11

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](https://docs.rs/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```
## Performance and Conformance

There used to be a statement here saying that performance is not the main goal of this crate. It is definitely one of them now.

While this crate doesn't provide a way to parse JSON to native Rust structs, it does a
lot to optimize its performance for DOM parsing, stringifying and manipulation. It does
[very well in benchmarks](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark), in some cases it
can even outperform parsing to structs.

This crate implements the standard according to the [
RFC 7159](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7159) and
[ECMA-404](http://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf)
documents. For the best interoperability numbers are treated stored as 64bit precision
mantissa with 16 bit decimal exponent for floating point representation.

This crate is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0). Choose whichever one works best for you.

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](http://json.rs/doc/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```
## Performance and Conformance

There used to be a statement here saying that performance is not the main goal of this crate. It is definitely one of them now.

While this crate doesn't provide a way to parse JSON to native Rust structs, it does a
lot to optimize it's performance for DOM parsing, stringifying and manipulation. It does
[very well in benchmarks](http://json.rs/), in some cases it
can even outperform parsing to structs.

This crate implements the standard according to the [
RFC 7159](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7159) and
[ECMA-404](http://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf)
documents. For the best interoperability numbers are treated stored as 64bit precision
mantissa with 16 bit decimal exponent for floating point representation.

## License

This crate is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0), choose whatever works for you.

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

---

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Changelog](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/releases) -[Complete Documentation](http://terhix.com/doc/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```
## Performance and Conformance

There used to be a statement here saying that performance is not the main goal of this crate. It is definitely one of them now.

While this crate doesn't provide a way to parse JSON to native Rust structs, it does a
lot to optimize it's performance for DOM parsing, stringifying and manipulation. It does
[very well in benchmarks](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark), in some cases it
can even outperform parsing to structs.

This crate implements the standard according to the [
RFC 7159](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7159) and
[ECMA-404](http://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf)
documents. It makes some compromises when it comes to number precision, but they are
both within the specification and advised practices for best interoperability,
specifically those discussed in the RFC.

## License

This crate is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0), choose whatever works for you.

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) for details.

[Complete Documentation](http://terhix.com/doc/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

# json 0.8.8 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.8.8

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Complete Documentation](http://terhix.com/doc/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```
## Performance

While performance is not the main goal of this crate, it is still relevant, and it's doing pretty well in the company:

[The benchmarks](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/blob/benches/benches/log.rs) were run on 2012 MacBook Air, your results may vary. Many thanks to [@dtolnay](https://github.com/dtolnay) for providing the baseline struct and test data the tests could be run on.

While this is not necessarily a be-all end-all benchmark, the main takeaway from this is that Serde parsing is much faster when parsing to a struct, since the parser knows exactly the kind of data it needs, and doesn't pay the (re)allocation costs of pushing data to a map. Also worth noting, rustc-serialize suffers since it first has to parse JSON to generic enum-based values, and only then map those onto structs.

---

## Performance

While performance is not the main goal of this crate, it is still relevant, and it's doing pretty well in the company:

[The benchmarks](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust/blob/benches/benches/log.rs) were run on 2012 MacBook Air, your results may vary. Many thanks to [@dtolnay](https://github.com/dtolnay) for providing the baseline struct and test data the tests could be run on.

While this is not necessarily a be-all end-all benchmark, the main takeaway from this is that Serde parsing is much faster when parsing to a struct, since the parser knows exactly the kind of data it needs, and doesn't pay the (re)allocation costs of pushing data to a map. Also worth noting, rustc-serialize suffers since it first has to parse JSON to generic enum-based values, and only then map those onto structs.

---

# json 0.8.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.8.5

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Complete Documentation](http://terhix.com/doc/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction.

```
let parsed = parse.unwrap;
let instantiated = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
## First class citizen

Using macros and indexing, it's easy to work with the data.

```
let mut data = object!;
// Partial equality is implemented for most raw types:
assert!;
// And it's type aware, `null` and `false` are different values:
assert!;
// But you can use any Rust number types:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Access nested structures, arrays and objects:
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient - accessing properties that don't exist yield null:
assert!;
// Mutate by assigning:
data = "Hello".into;
// Use the `dump` method to serialize the data:
assert_eq!;
// Or pretty print it out:
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```

While this is not necessarily a be-all end-all benchmark, the main takeaway from this is that Serde parsing is much faster when parsing to a struct, since the parser knows exactly the kind of data it needs, and doesn't pay the (re)allocation costs of pushing data to a map. # json 0.7.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.7.2

# json-rust

Parse and serialize [JSON](http://json.org/) with ease.

[Complete Documentation](http://terhix.com/doc/json/) -[Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) -[Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction by extensively using static dispatch and hiding type information behind enums, while still giving you all the guarantees of safe Rust code.

```
let data = parse.unwrap;
assert!;
assert!);
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient: non-existent values default to null
assert!;
```
## Create JSON data without defining structs

```
extern crate json;
```
## Mutate simply by assigning new values

```
let mut data = parse.unwrap;
data = true.into;
data = "Rust".into;
assert_eq!;
// Pretty print the output
println!;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```

---

# json 0.3.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.3.4

# JSON in Rust

Parse and serialize JSON with ease.

[Complete Documentation](http://terhix.com/doc/json/) - [Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) - [Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

# Why?

JSON is a very loose format where anything goes - arrays can hold mixed types, object keys can change types between API calls or not include some keys under some conditions. Mapping that to idiomatic Rust structs introduces friction.

This crate intends to avoid that friction by using extensive static dispatch and hiding type information behind enums, while still giving you all the safety guarantees of safe Rust code.

```
let data = parse.unwrap;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// Error resilient: non-existent values default to null
assert!;
```
## Easily create JSON data without defining structs

```
extern crate json;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```

---

# 🦄 JSON in Rust

# json 0.3.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.3.2

# 🦄 JSON in Rust

Parse and serialize JSON with ease.

[Complete Documentation](http://terhix.com/doc/json/) - [Cargo](https://crates.io/crates/json) - [Repository](https://github.com/maciejhirsz/json-rust)

## Easily access data without using structs.

```
extern crate json;
use JsonValue;
```
## Installation

Just add it to your `Cargo.toml` file:

```
[]
 = "*"
```
Then import it in your `main.rs` / `lib.rs` file:

```
extern crate json;
```

# json 0.3.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/json/0.3.1

# JSON in Rust

Parse and serialize JSON with ease.

```
extern crate json;
use JsonValue;
```
## Serialize with `json::stringify(value)`

Primitives:

```
// str slices
assert_eq!;
// Owned strings
assert_eq!;
// Any number types
assert_eq!;
// Booleans
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
Explicit `null` type `json::Null`:

```
assert_eq!;
```
Optional types:

```
let value:  = Some;
assert_eq!;
let no_value:  = None;
assert_eq!;
```
Vector:

```
let data = vec!;
assert_eq!;
```
Vector with optional values:

```
let data = vec!;
assert_eq!;
```
Pushing to arrays:

```
let mut data = new_array;
data.push;
data.push;
data.push;
assert_eq!;
```
Putting fields on objects:

```
let mut data = new_object;
data.put;
data.put;
assert_eq!;
```
`array!` macro:

```
let data = array!;
assert_eq!;
```
`object!` macro:

```
let data = object!;
assert_eq!;
```
